ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A certain laboratory keeps wild-type and some mutant fruit flies. Some recessive mutant genes of fruit flies and their positions on chromosomes are shown in the figure. Answer the question: Student B crossed singed-bristle white-eye male flies with wild-type (straight-bristle red-eye) homozygous female flies (forward cross). At this time, the probability that singed-bristle individuals appear among the male offspring is 0. If a reciprocal cross is carried out, what is the probability that white-eye individuals appear among the offspring?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure marks the positions of some recessive mutant genes of fruit flies on chromosomes: on the X chromosome are w (white eye) and sn (singed bristle); on chromosome No. 2 are dp (outstretched wing) and pr (purple eye); on chromosome No. 3 are ru (rough eye) and e (ebony body). Therefore, the white-eye gene w and the singed-bristle gene sn are both located on the X chromosome, and the stem states that these mutant genes are recessive. Reasoning: The forward cross is singed-bristle white-eye male fly × wild-type homozygous female fly. The genotype of the singed-bristle white-eye male fly can be represented as X^(sn w)Y, and the wild-type homozygous female fly as X^+X^+. In the offspring of the forward cross, male flies obtain X^+ from the mother and Y from the father, so the male offspring are X^+Y and do not show the recessive singed-bristle trait, which conforms to the stem’s “the probability that singed-bristle individuals appear among the male offspring is 0.” In the reciprocal cross, singed-bristle white-eye homozygous female flies X^(sn w)X^(sn w) are crossed with wild-type male flies X^+Y. Their female offspring are X^+X^(sn w); since white eye is recessive, they show red eyes. The male offspring are X^(sn w)Y and show white eyes. Since the sex ratio is about 1:1, the probability of white-eye individuals among all offspring is 1/2.
